acts.title: Scenario 1 · Recovery: automatic vs on request

compare.adk: Google ADK supports resuming interrupted agent executions, but its documented resumability mechanism <mark>requires an explicit resume request using the original invocation ID</mark>.
compare.temporal: Temporal's durable execution keeps a Workflow's state and progress through crashes and outages: any available Worker picks it up from the last recorded event in its history, <mark>with no resume request from your code</mark>.

temporal_source.label: Temporal docs: What is Temporal? · Durable Execution

steps.title: Set the stage: two of everything, no supervisor
steps.caption:
Both columns run the same agent with three tools. Left: ADK with resumability and a persistent session DB. Right: the same agent in a Temporal Workflow, where the ADK plugin makes every model and tool call an Activity.Read the code: the ADK setupthe Temporal setup
ADK has a spare, host B. Temporal's spare, Worker B, starts after Worker A dies. Auto-restart is off. Both sides crash just before emailing the customer: what continues the work?

steps.title: Refund $500 on ADK: host A dies before the email
steps.caption:
ADK host A takes the request, refunds and records the refund, then dies just before notify_customer.

Now watch the column: host B is healthy and idle, and the invocation sits unfinished in the shared session database. An ADK host only works on invocations it is asked to run, so nothing picks it up. Click Who resumes? to see the code you would have to write.

steps.title: Run the recovery scan you wrote
steps.caption:
Your turn: click Run recovery scan + resume in the ADK column. recovery.py resumes the invocation on host B, and the refund isn't repeated.

Now you own when the scan runs, dead vs slow (StaleSessionError), a lease, and code changed since the crash.ADK docs: resume ↗stopped workflows ↗

steps.title: The same refund on Temporal: Worker A dies before the email
steps.caption:
Same request, same crash point. Worker A refunds and records the refund (by Worker A on each step), then dies just before notify_customer.

No Worker is running now. The Workflow is not lost: its history and its next task wait on the Temporal Server.

steps.title: Start Worker B: it picks the work up
steps.caption:
Worker B picked it up: WorkflowTaskTimedOut, then WorkflowTaskStarted by worker-b, which replayed the history and sent the email. Earlier steps still read by Worker A: replay reused their results.

No scan, no lease, no resume call: the Temporal Server handed the work to the next Worker polling the task queue.Read more: Temporal docs: How a Worker processes a Workflow Task ↗

acts.title: Scenario 2 · Retries: durable vs in memory

compare.adk: Retries the model call in process, with retry_options as on Gemini. The attempt count and backoff live in the host's memory: kill the host and they are gone, and the invocation waits for your code.
compare.temporal: Retries the model Activity under a retry policy. <mark>The attempt count and the next retry time live on the Temporal Server</mark>, so a restarted Worker carries on at the next attempt.

adk_source.label: ADK docs: Gemini models · client-side retries

steps.title: Same retry schedule, kept in two places
steps.caption:
Both sides retry a failing model call on the same schedule: 1s, doubling, capped at 4s. ADK: the model's retry options, kept in the host's memory. Temporal: an Activity retry policy, scheduled by the Temporal Server.Read the code: ADK's retry optionsTemporal's retry policy
Auto-restart is on. ADK plays first, then Temporal, each with its own outage.

steps.title: The model is down: ADK retries in process
steps.caption: Every model call now fails with a 429 (overloaded), as during a provider incident. Watch LLM decides: in-process retry 2, 3… of 10. The page reads it from the host's log: an in-process retry writes nothing to the session database.

steps.title: Kill ADK host A mid-retry
steps.caption:
kill -9 on host A while it backs off; the supervisor restarts it. The outage ends a few seconds later.

The retry loop was a coroutine in the dead process. The restarted host knows nothing about it: model call never finished, and the invocation is unfinished. Its retries would have outlasted this outage if the process had lived. They died with it.

steps.title: Resume ADK
steps.caption:
Your turn again: click Run recovery scan + resume in the ADK column. The scan resumes it and the refund completes.

In-process retries are only as durable as the process: a crash during backoff leaves an unfinished invocation for your code to find.Read more: ADK docs: Gemini models · client-side retries ↗

steps.title: The same outage on Temporal: the Activity retries
steps.caption: The model is down again and the same refund starts on Temporal. Watch LLM decides: attempt 2, 3… on the pending Activity, held by the Temporal Server. So far, the same behaviour as ADK.

steps.title: Kill Worker A mid-retry
steps.caption:
kill -9 on Worker A while it backs off; the supervisor restarts it.

The next attempt was already scheduled on the Temporal Server, so Temporal finishes by itself: the attempt numbers carry on from before the crash, and no recovery code ran.Read more: Temporal docs: Retry Policies ↗

acts.title: Scenario 3 · Tool results: recorded on completion vs saved later

compare.adk: A tool's result is saved only when ADK writes its event. Crash after the payment, before that write, and the resume runs refund_payment again: two refunds.
compare.temporal: The Temporal Server records the Activity's result the moment it reports back, and replay reuses it: one refund. A crash inside the tool needs an idempotency key on both sides.

steps.title: A crash right after the side effect
steps.caption:
Back to one ADK host and one Worker, with auto-restart on. A crash point is armed on both sides: right after refund_payment returns, before the runtime records its result. The supervisor restarts dead processes, as Kubernetes would. No idempotency key yet.

Each crash plays on the ADK column first, then on the Temporal column.

steps.title: Refund $500 on ADK: host A dies right after the refund
steps.caption:
The agent decides to refund, calls refund_payment, the payment provider moves the money, and host A dies (os._exit, same as kill -9).

Watch refund_payment: money moved, result not recorded, because the crash came before the function response reached the session database. The supervisor restarted host A, and it is up and idle: as in Scenario 1, nothing told it an invocation was cut short.

steps.title: Resume the ADK invocation
steps.caption:
Click Run recovery scan + resume in the ADK column. ADK finds a call with no response (“Dropping function calls with no matching function response” in the log) and runs refund_payment again: $500 refunded twice.Read the code: how ADK resumes
Documented, not a bug: “we only guarantee an at-least-once behavior once resumed.”

steps.title: The same refund on Temporal: Worker A dies right after the refund
steps.caption:
Same crash point. refund_payment shows recorded: the Temporal Server wrote ActivityTaskCompleted the moment the Activity reported back.

Worker A restarted, polled the task queue and replayed the event history: the refund's result came from the history, so the agent went on to record it and email the customer. One refund; nobody resumed anything.

steps.title: A crash inside the tool, on ADK
steps.caption:
So is Temporal exactly-once? Let's check. A different crash point: inside refund_payment, after the money moved, before the tool returns. Neither runtime can know the money moved.

ADK host A dies and restarts idle again.

steps.title: Resume ADK: refunded twice
steps.caption:
Click Run recovery scan + resume in the ADK column, again.

The resume runs refund_payment again: $ moved ×2, the same as before.

steps.title: The same crash on Temporal: refunded twice too
steps.caption:
Temporal sees the dead Worker when the Activity's 6s start-to-close timeout passes, and retries: attempt 2, then $ moved ×2.

A completed Activity is recorded once and never re-run, but an Activity executes at least once: a crash inside it means a retry. No runtime makes an external side effect exactly-once alone; you need the payment provider's help.

steps.title: Turn on the idempotency key and crash ADK again
steps.caption: The tool now sends Idempotency-Key: <run id>:<function call id>. The function call id is stable on both runtimes: Temporal retries the Activity with the arguments recorded in the history, and ADK resumes with the function call it persisted (we checked: same id). A repeated key makes the provider return the original refund.

steps.title: Resume ADK: one refund
steps.caption:
Click Run recovery scan + resume in the ADK column, once more.

One refund, one deduplicated retry: the provider saw the same key and returned the original refund.

steps.title: The same crash on Temporal: one refund
steps.caption:
One refund, one deduplicated retry here too.

What's different: (1) Temporal's repeat window is only inside the Activity; ADK's also covers the gap before the session write, the first crash we saw. (2) Nobody resumed Temporal. (3) Retries, timeouts and backoff are declared per Activity (TOOL_OPTIONS), every attempt in the history.

acts.title: Scenario 4 · Timers: durable vs in memory

compare.adk: Pauses with tool confirmation, and the host enforces the deadline with an asyncio timer. The timer lives in the host's memory: stop the host and the deadline is never enforced.
compare.temporal: The same tool confirmation, plus a durable timer. <mark>The timer lives on the Temporal Server and fires with no Worker running</mark>; the next Worker escalates and denies.

adk_source.label: ADK docs: Tool confirmation with Resume

steps.title: A policy with a deadline
steps.caption:
Refunds over $250 need a manager's approval within 48 hours (20 seconds here); past the deadline, deny and escalate.

Both sides pause with ADK's tool confirmation. ADK: the host keeps the deadline as a timer in its memory. Temporal: the Workflow waits with a timeout, a durable timer.Read the code: ADK's pause and timerTemporal's wait
ADK plays first, then Temporal, each with a 20-second wait.

steps.title: Refund $500 on ADK: it waits for a manager
steps.caption: ADK ends the invocation in a paused state, saved in the session DB, and host A starts its deadline timer in memory (timer held in this process's memory in the log). No thread is held while it waits.

steps.title: Stop ADK host A during the wait
steps.caption: Host A is stopped. The paused invocation survives in the database, but its timer was an asyncio task in host A's memory: gone. Let the deadline pass.

steps.title: Past the deadline: bring host A back
steps.caption: Host A is running again and <mark class="weak">the refund is still paused</mark>. The restarted host doesn't know a deadline exists, so nobody escalates and nobody denies. Enforcing it needs a scheduler that persists every paused invocation's deadline, plus recovery code like Scenario 1's.

steps.title: A late approval still resumes ADK
steps.caption:
A manager approves after the deadline. ADK resumes and refunds $500: resumable, yes.

But the policy said deny and escalate at the deadline. Nothing acted, so a refund the policy should have denied went through. Resuming late is not acting on time.Read more: ADK docs: Tool confirmation with Resume ↗

steps.title: The same refund on Temporal: it waits for a manager
steps.caption: Temporal waits in workflow.wait_condition(…, timeout=deadline): TimerStarted in the history. Like ADK, no thread is held while it waits.

steps.title: Stop Worker A during the wait
steps.caption: Worker A is stopped: no Worker is running at all. The timer is a record on the Temporal Server, not memory in a process. Let the deadline pass and watch for TimerFired in the history.

steps.title: Past the deadline: bring Worker A back
steps.caption:
The timer fired on the Temporal Server with no Worker running. Worker A picks it up, opens a manager ticket, denies the refund and tells the customer: the except asyncio.TimeoutError branch in _await_manager.

Acting on time is a timeout and an exception handler, and the timer survives losing every Worker.Read more: Temporal docs: Durable timers ↗

compare.adk: A resumable agent: events are persisted, and it resumes by invocation ID when your code asks. Retries and timers live in a process's memory.
compare.temporal: A durable agent: recovery, retries, timers and tool results are durable, kept by the Temporal Server, with no resume request from your code.

steps.title: Durable execution, in four results
steps.caption:
Durable execution takes care of automated process recovery, durable retries, strongly consistent tool execution and durable timers, for the same agent.py.
Resumable agent
plain ADK		Durable agent
Temporal + ADK
Process recovery
Scenario 1		Your code finds unfinished invocations and sends an explicit resume request with the invocation ID.Automated. Any Worker on the task queue picks the work up and replays the history. No resume request.
Retries
Scenario 2		In process (retry_options). The attempt count and backoff die with the process.Durable. Attempt count and next retry time live on the Temporal Server, and carry on after a restart.
Tool execution
Scenario 3		A tool's result is saved when the host writes its event. A crash in between, and resume runs the tool again.Strongly consistent. The Temporal Server records each result the moment the Activity completes. Replay reuses it and never re-runs the tool.
Timers
Scenario 4		In process (asyncio), or a scheduler you build and run. Stop the host and the deadline is never enforced.Durable. The timer fires on the Temporal Server with no Worker running.

A crash inside a tool, after its side effect, means a retry on either runtime: give side-effecting tools an idempotency key (Scenario 3).

steps.title: Use them together
steps.caption:
Temporal owns the lifecycle of the business process; ADK owns the agent's reasoning and tool selection. This is the right-hand column of the demo, with agent.py unchanged.
Use caseRecommended
Conversational assistant with tool callingADK alone
Long-running agent with resumable reasoningADK resumability, or a managed agent runtime
Critical business process with agents, payments, approvals and external systemsTemporal + ADK

Either way, give side-effecting tools an idempotency key.

steps.title: Questions to ask any agent runtime
steps.caption:
Whichever runtime you evaluate, managed or self-hosted, ask these. The scenarios answer the first three for plain ADK and for Temporal; the tests cover the fourth.
  1. Crash consistency. A tool performs an external side effect, then the process dies before the checkpoint is written. What happens? Scenario 3
  2. Recovery ownership. After a host dies or a model call fails, what schedules the recovery? Does your application have to call resume? Where does a retry's state live while it backs off? Scenarios 1 and 2
  3. Durable waiting. Can an agent wait 30 days for an event without holding compute or a custom scheduler, and act when a deadline passes? Scenario 4
  4. Concurrent recovery. What stops two replicas from resuming the same execution at once? tests
  5. Execution guarantees. Which operations are replayed, which are retried, and which are guaranteed not to repeat after a recorded completion?
  6. Versioning. What happens to a three-week execution when the agent's prompts, tools or graph change?
  7. Integrity of what gets re-run. Who can change a stored tool call's arguments before a resume runs it?

In one line: ADK helps an agent continue its work after an interruption. Temporal helps the whole business transaction continue, even when the agent, its tools or the infrastructure fail. They are complementary.
